extracted.intended_audience: practitioners (attorneys and agents) who practice before the USPTO; Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) staff; law firms with USPTO practice
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules governing the ethical duties, disciplinary processes, status changes (inactive/resignation), and practice responsibilities of practitioners before the USPTO in patent matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice to ascertain desire to remain on register
rubrics_metrics.description: A letter may be addressed to any registered practitioner at the address of which separate notice was last received by the OED Director for the purpose of ascertaining whether such practitioner desires to remain on the register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any registered practitioner failing to reply and give any information requested by the OED Director within a time limit specified will be subject to administrative suspension under paragraph (b) of this section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative suspension — notice and delinquency fee
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever it appears a registered practitioner has failed to comply with certain address/notice requirements, the OED Director shall publish and send a notice advising of the noncompliance, the consequence of administrative suspension if noncompliance is not timely remedied, and the requirements for reinstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice shall demand compliance and payment of a delinquency fee set forth in § 1.21(a)(9)(i) within sixty days after the date of such notice; notice shall be mailed to last postal address or emailed to last email address furnished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule to Show Cause for administrative suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: If the practitioner fails to comply with the notice within the time allowed, the OED Director shall publish and send a Rule to Show Cause why his or her registration or recognition should not be administratively suspended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Rule to Show Cause will state that the person will no longer be permitted to practice before the Office in patent matters or hold himself/herself out as registered; OED Director files copy with USPTO Director.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response to Rule to Show Cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Within 30 days of the Rule to Show Cause being sent, the practitioner may file a response with the USPTO Director setting forth factual and legal bases why the person should not be administratively suspended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practitioner must serve the OED Director with a copy when filed; OED Director may file a reply within ten days including documents demonstrating proper notice was published and sent.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Director action on Rule to Show Cause
rubrics_metrics.description: When acting on a Rule to Show Cause, if the USPTO Director determines there are no genuine issues of material fact regarding the Office’s compliance with notice requirements or the failure to pay requisite fees, the USPTO Director shall enter an order administratively suspending the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If genuine issues exist, the USPTO Director shall enter an appropriate order dismissing the Rule to Show Cause. An administratively suspended practitioner may not seek a stay of the suspension during review of the Director’s final decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation and discipline while administratively suspended
rubrics_metrics.description: An administratively suspended practitioner is subject to investigation and discipline for conduct prior to, during, or after the period of administrative suspension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An administratively suspended practitioner is prohibited from practicing before the Office in patent cases while administratively suspended; knowingly practicing while suspended is grounds for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative inactivation for Office employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Any registered practitioner who becomes employed by the Office must withdraw from matters they represent and notify the OED Director on the first day of employment; their name will be endorsed on the roster as administratively inactive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon separation from the Office, the practitioner may request reactivation by completing an application, Data Sheet, signing undertaking required by § 11.10, and paying fees; administratively inactive practitioners remain subject to Rules of Professional Conduct and to proceedings/sanctions for conduct prior to or during employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative inactivation for judges and similar
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered practitioner who is a judge or certain judicial officers may request endorsement as administratively inactive if not engaged in the practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following separation from the bench, the practitioner may request restoration to active status by completing application, Data Sheet, and signing required undertaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary inactive status
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered practitioner may be placed on voluntary inactive status and is prohibited from practicing before the Office in patent cases while in that status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner in voluntary inactive status is subject to discipline for failing to comply with provisions governing inactive status; upon acceptance practitioner must comply with § 11.116.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration from voluntary inactive status
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner whose name was endorsed as voluntarily inactive and who is not under investigation or subject to disciplinary proceeding may be restored to active status provided they file a written request for restoration, a completed application, Data Sheet, information on moral character and reputation during inactivation, a declaration attesting they have read most recent revisions of patent laws and rules, and pay specified fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restoration requires submission of requested materials and payment of fees set forth in §§ 1.21(a)(7)(iii) and (iv).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resignation procedure and continuing jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered practitioner not under investigation or certain disciplinary processes may resign by notifying the OED Director in writing; upon acceptance the practitioner is no longer eligible to practice before the Office in patent matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resigned practitioners must continue to file a change of address for five years so they may be located if information about prior conduct comes to light; resignation acceptance requires compliance with § 11.116 and results in removal from the register with notice published in the Official Gazette. Practitioners who have resigned remain subject to disciplinary jurisdiction for prior conduct and conduct following resignation regarding practice before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary jurisdiction scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office has disciplinary jurisdiction over all practitioners engaged in practice before the Office, administratively suspended practitioners, inactivated practitioners, practitioners authorized under § 11.6(d) to take testimony, practitioners transferred to disability inactive status, reprimanded, suspended, or excluded practitioners, and practitioners suspended/excluded from practice by other duly constituted authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners who have resigned are subject to jurisdiction with respect to conduct undertaken prior to resignation and conduct in regard to any practice before the Office following resignation; a person not registered is also subject to disciplinary authority if providing or offering to provide any legal services before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary sanctions — probation
rubrics_metrics.description: Probation may be imposed in lieu of or in addition to any other disciplinary sanction; any conditions of probation must be stated in writing in the order imposing probation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order must state whether and to what extent the practitioner must notify clients of probation; violation of any condition of probation is cause for imposition of disciplinary sanction only after an order to show cause is resolved adversely to the practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions imposed with discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: When imposing discipline, the USPTO Director may condition reinstatement upon the practitioner making restitution, successfully completing a professional responsibility course or examination, or any other condition deemed appropriate under the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warnings as non-public dispositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A warning is neither public nor a disciplinary sanction; the OED Director may conclude an investigation with issuance of a warning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The warning shall contain a brief statement of facts and USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct relevant to the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation information from non-grieving clients
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director may request information and evidence regarding possible grounds for discipline from a non-grieving client after obtaining the practitioner’s consent or upon a Contact Member finding good cause to believe the alleged ground has occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither a request for, nor disclosure of, such information shall constitute a violation of any USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline — effect of adjudication elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: A final adjudication in another jurisdiction or Federal agency that a practitioner has been guilty of misconduct establishes a prima facie case by clear and convincing evidence that the practitioner has engaged in misconduct under § 11.804.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim suspension based on conviction of serious crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon conviction of a crime in any court, a practitioner must notify the OED Director in writing within thirty days; the OED Director shall determine whether the crime constitutes a serious crime warranting interim suspension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the crime is serious, the OED Director will file proof of conviction with the USPTO Director and request issuance of a notice and order and file a complaint predicated upon the conviction; if not a serious crime, the matter will be processed like other information of possible rule violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instituting a disciplinary proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: If after conducting an investigation the OED Director is of the opinion grounds exist for discipline, the OED Director may convene a panel of the Committee on Discipline to determine whether probable cause exists to bring disciplinary charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the panel determines probable cause exists, the OED Director may institute a disciplinary proceeding by filing a complaint under § 11.34.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaint content sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A complaint instituting a disciplinary proceeding must name the person who is the subject (the respondent) and will be deemed sufficient if it fairly informs the respondent of any grounds for discipline and, where applicable, the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct that form the basis so the respondent can adequately prepare a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service of complaint — address rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Service provisions include rules for serving a respondent who is not registered at the last address for the respondent known to the OED Director.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial decision of hearing officer — remedies and transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: A hearing officer’s initial decision may order default judgment, suspension or exclusion, reprimand, probation, or dismiss the complaint and may impose any conditions appropriate under the circumstances; the decision shall be transmitted to the OED Director and respondent and the entire record transmitted to the OED Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the absence of an appeal to the USPTO Director, the hearing officer’s decision becomes the decision of the USPTO Director thirty days from the date of the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial decision — explanation of sanctions and sentencing factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial decision shall explain the reason for any default judgment, reprimand, suspension, exclusion, or probation and explain any conditions imposed with discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In determining any sanction, four factors must be considered if applicable (factors not fully listed in this chunk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties following suspension/exclusion/resignation — affidavit of compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Within forty-five days after entry of the order of suspension, exclusion, or acceptance of resignation, the practitioner shall file with the OED Director an affidavit of compliance certifying full compliance with the provisions of the order, this section, and § 11.116 for withdrawal from representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appended to the affidavit shall be specified materials (details not all included in this chunk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden to show compliance for reinstatement
rubrics_metrics.description: A suspended, excluded, or resigned practitioner must show by clear and convincing evidence that they have complied with the provisions of the relevant duties section and all USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct in order to be reinstated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated responsibilities and rule headings (Subpart D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subpart D lists multiple subject areas governing practitioner responsibilities including: responsibilities of partners/managers/supervisory practitioners; subordinate practitioner responsibilities; responsibilities regarding non-practitioner assistants; professional independence; unauthorized practice of law; restrictions on right to practice; law-related services; client-practitioner relationship topics (competence, scope, diligence, communication, fees, confidentiality, conflicts, duties to former clients, imputation); counselor and advocate roles; transactions with persons other than clients; information about legal services; maintaining integrity of the profession (registration, reporting, misconduct); and saving clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These headings indicate the topics containing substantive standards and duties later set forth in the rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall provide competent representation to a client. Competent representation requires the legal, scientific, and technical knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of representation and allocation of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall abide by a client’s decisions concerning the objectives of representation and, as required by § 11.104, shall consult with the client as to the means by which they are to be pursued; a practitioner may take such action as is impliedly authorized to carry out the representation and shall abide by a client’s decision whether to settle a matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner may limit the scope of the representation if the limitation is reasonable and the client gives informed consent. A practitioner shall not counsel or assist a client in conduct the practitioner knows is criminal or fraudulent, but may discuss legal consequences and help make good-faith determinations of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication with client
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall: (1) promptly inform the client of any decision or circumstance requiring the client’s informed consent; (2) reasonably consult with the client about the means to accomplish objectives; (3) keep the client reasonably informed about status; (4) promptly comply with reasonable requests for information; and (5) consult with the client about limitations on practitioner conduct when the client expects assistance not permitted by rules or law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner shall explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees — reasonableness and factors
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not make an agreement for, charge, or collect an unreasonable fee or an unreasonable amount for expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider in determining reasonableness include: time and labor required; novelty and difficulty of questions and requisite skill; likelihood acceptance will preclude other employment; customary fee in locality for similar services; amount involved and results obtained; time limitations imposed; nature and length of relationship; experience, reputation, and ability of practitioner(s); and whether the fee is fixed or contingent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees — communication and contingent fee requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of representation and the basis or rate of the fee and expenses should be communicated to the client, preferably in writing, before or within a reasonable time after commencing representation. Contingent fees are permitted except where prohibited by law and must be in writing signed by the client and detail the method of calculation, deductions, and client liabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon conclusion of a contingent fee matter the practitioner shall provide a written statement stating the outcome and, if there is a recovery, showing remittance to the client and the method of its determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of fees between practitioners not in same firm
rubrics_metrics.description: A division of a fee between practitioners not in the same firm may be made only if the division is in proportion to services performed or each assumes joint responsibility; the client agrees including the share each will receive and the agreement is confirmed in writing; and the total fee is reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of information — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not reveal information relating to the representation of a client unless the client gives informed consent, disclosure is impliedly authorized to carry out the representation, disclosure is permitted under enumerated exceptions, or disclosure is required by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality — permitted disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may reveal information to the extent reasonably necessary to: prevent reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm; prevent the client from committing a crime, fraud, or inequitable conduct before the Office reasonably certain to result in substantial injury to financial interests or property and in furtherance of which the client used the practitioner’s services; prevent, mitigate, or rectify such substantial injury; secure legal advice about compliance with the rules; establish a claim or defense on behalf of the practitioner; or comply with other law or a court order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose to the Office
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall disclose to the Office information necessary to comply with applicable duty of disclosure provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest — concurrent conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not represent a client if the representation involves a concurrent conflict of interest: (1) the representation of one client will be directly adverse to another; or (2) there is a significant risk the representation will be materially limited by responsibilities to another client, a former client, a third person, or by a personal interest of the practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest — informed-consent exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding a concurrent conflict, a practitioner may represent a client if: (1) the practitioner reasonably believes they will provide competent and diligent representation to each affected client; (2) the representation is not prohibited by law; (3) the representation does not involve assertion of a claim by one client against another client represented by the practitioner in the same litigation or proceeding; and (4) each affected client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business transactions with clients
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not enter into a business transaction with a client or knowingly acquire an ownership or pecuniary interest adverse to a client unless the transaction and terms are fair and reasonable to the client and fully disclosed in writing in a manner reasonably understood by the client; the client is advised in writing of desirability of seeking independent counsel and given reasonable opportunity; and the client gives informed consent in a signed writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of client information to client’s disadvantage
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not use information relating to representation to the disadvantage of the client unless the client gives informed consent, or as the Rules would permit or require.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation of substantial gifts
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not solicit any substantial gift from a client, including a testamentary gift, or prepare on behalf of a client an instrument giving the practitioner or a related person any substantial gift unless related to the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related persons include spouse, child, grandchild, parent, grandparent or other relative or individual with whom the practitioner maintains a close familial relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary or media rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to conclusion of representation, a practitioner shall not make or negotiate an agreement giving the practitioner literary or media rights to a portrayal or account based in substantial part on information relating to the representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial assistance to client
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not provide financial assistance to a client in connection with pending or contemplated litigation except that: (1) a practitioner may advance court costs and expenses of litigation repayable contingent on outcome; and (2) a practitioner representing an indigent client may pay court costs and expenses on behalf of the client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation from third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not accept compensation for representing a client from one other than the client unless the client gives informed consent; there is no interference with the practitioner’s independence of professional judgment or the client-practitioner relationship; and information relating to representation is protected as required by § 11.106.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate settlements
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who represents two or more clients shall not participate in making an aggregate settlement of claims of or against the clients unless each client gives informed consent in writing signed by the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practitioner’s disclosure must include the existence and nature of all claims involved and the participation of each person in the settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting malpractice liability and settling with unrepresented clients
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not make an agreement prospectively limiting the practitioner’s liability to a client for malpractice unless the client is independently represented in making the agreement; and shall not settle a claim for such liability with an unrepresented client or former client unless that person is advised in writing of desirability of seeking and given reasonable opportunity to seek independent counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proprietary interest in cause of action or subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not acquire a proprietary interest in the cause of action, subject matter of litigation, or a proceeding before the Office which the practitioner is conducting for a client, except that a practitioner may: (1) acquire a lien authorized by law to secure fees or expenses; (2) contract for a reasonable contingent fee in a civil case; and (3) in a patent case or proceeding before the Office, take an interest in the patent as part or all of his or her fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm-wide application of prohibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: While practitioners are associated in a firm, a prohibition that applies to any one of them under certain paragraphs shall apply to all of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties to former clients
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who has formerly represented a client in a matter shall not thereafter represent another person in the same or a substantially related matter materially adverse to the former client unless the former client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also bars representation when the practitioner acquired protected information at a former firm about a former client unless former client gives informed consent confirmed in writing; prohibits using or revealing information relating to prior representation to the disadvantage of the former client except as permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imputation of conflicts — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: While practitioners are associated in a firm, none shall knowingly represent a client when any one of them practicing alone would be prohibited by §§ 11.107 or 11.109 unless exceptions apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions include (1) prohibition based on a personal interest of the disqualified practitioner that does not present significant risk of materially limiting representation by remaining practitioners; or (2) prohibition based upon prior-firm association where (i) the disqualified practitioner is timely screened and apportioned no part of the fee; (ii) written notice promptly given to affected former client describing screening procedures, stating compliance, stating review may be available before a tribunal, and agreeing to respond to inquiries; and (iii) certifications of compliance with screening (text continues).
